2.5: "Desirous of gain" is read here as describing the teachers. It can also describe the enjoyments: "enjoyments of wealth and pleasure, smeared with blood".
2.7: "For certain" is taken with "tell me". It can also go with "better": "tell me what is decidedly better".
2.9: "O scorcher of foes" follows this text, where Sañjaya addresses the king. Other copies of the text read it as describing Arjuna: "the scorcher of foes fell silent".
2.13: The word translated "steadfast" (dhīra) can equally mean "wise".
2.15: The word translated "steadfast" (dhīra) can equally mean "wise".
2.16: "The end" can also be read as "the conclusion": the settled truth about what is and what is not.
2.20: The second line has several negatives and can be divided differently, giving "having come to be, it will not come to be again".
2.21: The last part is two literal questions. It is usually understood as one: "how can that person slay anyone, or cause anyone to be slain?"
2.29: "As a wonder" is taken to describe what is seen. It can also describe the seeing, or the rare person who sees.
2.38: "Yoke yourself" keeps the root of the word yoga. The plainer sense is "make ready for battle".
2.39: "In sāṅkhya" and "in yoga" are read as the names of two teachings. They can also be read as "with regard to understanding" and "with regard to practice".
2.42: Verses 42 to 44 are one sentence in the Sanskrit. A few words are repeated here so that each verse reads as a full sentence.
2.45: "Standing in sattva" reads sattva as one of the three guṇas. It can also mean "standing in true being", which sits more easily beside "free of the three guṇas".
2.46: This verse is read two ways. One: the Vedas are of as little use to one who knows as a well is in a flood. The other: everything a well gives is contained in a flood, and likewise everything in the Vedas is contained in what the knower knows.
2.50: The last phrase can also be read the other way round: "skill in actions is yoga".
2.53: "Perplexed by what is heard" can also be read as "turned away from what is heard". "What is heard" means revealed scripture.
2.54: The three questions are read as "how": how would he speak, sit and walk. They can also be read as "what would he say", or as plain questions.
2.59: "Who takes no food" is the literal sense. It is often understood as "who does not feed the senses on their objects".
2.61: "Yoked" keeps the root of the word yoga. The plainer sense is "disciplined".
2.67: "That" is read here as the mind. It can also be whichever sense the mind follows: that one sense carries the understanding away.
2.72: "The nirvāṇa of brahman" can also be read as "nirvāṇa in brahman" or "the nirvāṇa that is brahman".
6.1: "Without rites" can also be read simply as "without action".
6.3: "The means" can also be read as "the cause".
6.7: "The highest self" reads paramātmā as one word. Divided as two words it gives "the self is exceedingly collected".
6.11: Verses 11 and 12 are one sentence in the Sanskrit. "A seat for the self" simply means "his own seat".
6.13: Verses 13 and 14 are one sentence in the Sanskrit.
6.17: "Measured" translates yukta, the word translated "yoked" in nearby verses. Both senses are present.
6.20: Verses 20 to 23 are one sentence in the Sanskrit.
6.21: "Does not move from the truth" can also be read as "truly does not move".
6.24: Verses 24 and 25 are one sentence in the Sanskrit.
6.28: "The touch of brahman" can also be read as describing the happiness: "happiness that consists in contact with brahman". "With ease" can also be read as "by happiness".
6.31: "Living in every way" can also be read as "in whatever condition he exists".
6.32: "By likeness to the self" means by comparing others with oneself. "Sees the same" can also be read as "sees equally".
6.36: "Through the right means" can also be read as a second "by one who strives".
6.38: "Fallen from both" leaves "both" unnamed, as the Sanskrit does. It is usually understood as the path of action and the path of yoga.
6.44: "The brahman of words" is the literal sense. It is traditionally understood as the Vedas and their rites.
6.47: "Of all yogīs" can also be read as "compared with all yogīs".
